key_terms.meaning: A = U − TS, with U internal energy, T absolute temperature, S entropy; natural variables T and V
G = H − TS = A + PV, with H enthalpy and P pressure; natural variables T and P
A change of independent variable made by subtracting a product of conjugate variables, e.g. TS or PV, from a potential
−ΔA is the maximum work at constant T and V; −ΔG is the maximum non-PV work at constant T and P
dU = TdS − PdV, dH = TdS + VdP, dA = −SdT − PdV, dG = −SdT + VdP
A differential whose mixed second partial derivatives are equal, so its value depends only on the end states
(∂(G/T)/∂T)_P = −H/T², linking the temperature change of G to H
Four equalities such as (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V, obtained from exactness of the potentials
μ = (∂T/∂P)_H; positive μ means cooling on throttling
Mᴿ = M − M^ig, the difference between a real-fluid property and its ideal-gas value at the same T and P
Another name for a residual property, usually written for H, S, G and V
x = mass of vapour ÷ total mass in a two-phase mixture, ranging from 0 to 1
The condition where liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium at a given P or T
dP^sat/dT = ΔH_vap/(T·ΔV), the slope of a saturation curve
Cp − Cv = −T(∂P/∂T)_V² ÷ (∂P/∂V)_T, zero only for an ideal gas
γ = Cp/Cv, equal to 1 for an ideal gas only if Cp = Cv, and about 1.4 for diatomic ideal gases
κ = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)_T, a positive PVT derivative used in many identities
Writing a partial derivative as ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y) so that chain rules and variable swaps follow algebraically

takeaways: Free energies exist because at fixed T and V, or fixed T and P, part of the internal energy is unavailable as work.
All thermodynamic relations for a pure fluid follow from just two statements: energy conservation and the entropy inequality.
Maxwell relations turn entropy derivatives, which cannot be measured, into P–V–T derivatives, which can.
Residual properties are the bridge between an equation of state and the steam tables, because both are measured from the same ideal-gas reference.
Inside the saturation dome every specific property is a straight-line mixture of saturated liquid and saturated vapour values, weighted by quality.
The Clausius–Clapeyron equation predicts how boiling point shifts with pressure, which is why a pressure cooker cooks faster.
Cp − Cv is zero for an ideal gas and positive for every real fluid, and its size comes purely from PVT data.
The Jacobian method removes guesswork: any partial derivative can be reduced to P, V, T, Cp and Cv by a fixed recipe.
bank_note: Long answers here are mostly derivations, so the syllabi reward a clean statement of the starting relation, each differentiation step, and a final interpretation in measurable P–V–T and heat-capacity terms.

bank.q: State the four fundamental property relations for U, H, A and G. Explain what the natural variables of each potential are and why that pair is natural.
outline: Write dU = TdS − PdV, dH = TdS + VdP, dA = −SdT − PdV, dG = −SdT + VdP.
Define every symbol with units: U, H, A, G in kJ/mol; T in K; P in kPa; V in m³/mol; S in kJ/(mol·K).
Show dH = dU + d(PV) and dA = dU − d(T S) and dG = dH − d(T S).
Natural variables: U(S,V), H(S,P), A(T,V), G(T,P); the differential then gives the conjugate partial derivatives directly.
Note that G is the convenient potential for constant-T, constant-P chemical processes.

bank.q: Explain why the Helmholtz and Gibbs free energies are called Legendre transforms, and interpret the work they measure at constant T,V and at constant T,P.
outline: Start from U(S,V) and the desire to use T instead of S as independent variable.
Subtract TS to get A; subtract TS and add PV to get G.
Show that for an isothermal change at constant T, w_max = −ΔA.
Show that for a constant-T, constant-P change, non-PV work maximum = −ΔG.
Give one example such as a battery or a reversible cell where ΔG sets the maximum electrical work.

bank.q: Define a residual property and explain why the ideal-gas state at the same temperature and pressure is chosen as the reference rather than the ideal-gas state at the same temperature and volume.
outline: Definition Mᴿ = M − M^ig at the same T and P.
Residual property tends to zero as P tends to zero, which gives a clean integration limit.
Properties of the ideal-gas state depend only on T, so M^ig is easy to compute from Cp^ig.
Work with Gᴿ because ln φ = Gᴿ/(RT) connects residuals to fugacity coefficient.
Mention that Hᴿ and Sᴿ come from integrating an equation of state in P at fixed T.

bank.q: Write the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, state the assumptions used to obtain its integrated form, and derive that integrated form.
outline: Start with dP^sat/dT = ΔH_vap/(T ΔV).
State ΔV ≈ V_vap when the liquid volume is neglected.
Assume the vapour is ideal so V_vap = RT/P^sat.
Assume ΔH_vap constant over the range to get ln(P2/P1) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1).
Give one use: estimating latent heat from a plot of ln P^sat against 1/T.

bank.q: Using the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂P/∂T)_V, derive the internal-pressure expression (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂P/∂T)_V − P, and evaluate it for a gas obeying P(V − b) = RT.
outline: Begin from dU = TdS − PdV, divide by dV at constant T.
Substitute the Maxwell relation.
Differentiate the equation of state to get (∂P/∂T)_V = R/(V − b).
Substitute to obtain (∂U/∂V)_T = RT/(V − b) − P = bP²/(RT) for this model.
Conclude the ideal-gas limit b = 0 gives zero internal pressure, so U depends on T only.

bank.q: Derive the general relation Cp − Cv = −T(∂P/∂T)_V² ÷ (∂P/∂V)_T and show its value for an ideal gas and for a van der Waals gas.
outline: Start from Cp − Cv = [P + (∂U/∂V)_T](∂V/∂T)_P.
Use the internal-pressure result and the cyclic relation to convert (∂V/∂T)_P.
Obtain the final formula and check the ideal-gas case gives zero.
For van der Waals, evaluate (∂P/∂T)_V = R/(V − b) and (∂P/∂V)_T.
Discuss that Cp − Cv rises sharply near the critical point.

bank.q: Use the Jacobian method to express the derivative (∂H/∂P)_T in terms of measurable quantities, stating each rule used at every step.
outline: Write (∂H/∂P)_T = ∂(H,T)/∂(P,T).
Replace H by H(T,P) and expand the Jacobian by the chain rule.
Use ∂(H,T)/∂(P,T) = (∂H/∂T)_P = Cp.
So (∂H/∂P)_T = Cp (∂T/∂P)_H, i.e. −Cp μ where μ is the Joule–Thomson coefficient.
Alternatively obtain −Cp μ = V − T(∂V/∂T)_P and check it vanishes for an ideal gas.

bank.q: Steam at 0.5 MPa has a quality of 0.85. Using saturated-steam table values, calculate its specific volume, specific enthalpy and specific entropy, and state the assumption used.
outline: Read v_f, v_g, h_f, h_g, s_f, s_g at 0.5 MPa from the tables.
Apply M = M_f + x(M_g − M_f) for each property.
Carry units: v in m³/kg, h in kJ/kg, s in kJ/(kg·K).
State that the mixture is in equilibrium and homogeneous in pressure and temperature.
Note the result must lie between the saturated liquid and saturated vapour values.

bank.q: A vapour-pressure data set for a pure liquid gives ln P^sat against 1/T as a straight line of slope −4200 K. Estimate the latent heat of vaporisation and explain the assumptions behind the estimate.
outline: Use slope = −ΔH_vap/R from the integrated Clausius–Clapeyron equation.
Convert units carefully because R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
State the assumptions: ideal vapour, negligible liquid volume, constant ΔH_vap, negligible non-ideality.
Comment that the estimate is an average over the temperature range.
Mention that a curved plot means ΔH_vap varies with temperature.

bank.q: Starting from the residual Gibbs energy obtained from a cubic equation of state, outline the steps to compute the fugacity coefficient of a pure gas, and state how the result is checked.
outline: Write ln φ = Gᴿ/(RT) = ∫0^P (Z − 1) dP/P at constant T.
Substitute the equation of state in compressibility form and integrate.
Show the low-pressure check: as P tends to 0, Z tends to 1 and φ tends to 1.
Compute Hᴿ and Sᴿ from related integrals using the same equation of state.
Note that at saturation the fugacities of liquid and vapour must be equal.

bank.q: Show from the Gibbs free energy that (∂Cp/∂P)_T = −T(∂²V/∂T²)_P, and use it to judge whether the heat capacity of a real gas can be treated as a function of temperature alone.
outline: Start from dG = −SdT + VdP and cross-differentiate to get (∂S/∂P)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_P.
Differentiate both sides with respect to T at constant P.
Use Cp = T(∂S/∂T)_P to reach the required result.
For an ideal gas V = RT/P gives zero pressure dependence.
For a real gas the second derivative of V is nonzero, so Cp depends on pressure; estimate the size of the effect at high pressure.

bank.q: Compare residual and excess properties. Explain when an equation of state with residual properties is preferred and when activity-coefficient models with excess properties are preferred, using a vapour–liquid equilibrium calculation as the example.
outline: Residual property compares real fluid with ideal gas at the same T and P; excess property compares real mixture with ideal solution at the same T, P and composition.
Residual properties come from an equation of state and suit the vapour phase and supercritical conditions.
Excess properties come from activity-coefficient models and suit the liquid phase at low pressure.
State the equilibrium condition: equality of fugacity in each phase, with φ for vapour and γ for liquid.
Note that both descriptions must agree at the critical region, where only the equation-of-state route works.

bank.q: Derive the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation from the fundamental relation for G, and evaluate its use in obtaining the temperature dependence of the equilibrium constant.
outline: Start from dG = −SdT + VdP and G = H − TS.
Divide by T and differentiate with respect to T at constant P to get (∂(G/T)/∂T)_P = −H/T².
Apply to each species and combine with ΔG° = −RT ln K.
Obtain d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/(RT²).
State that the sign of ΔH° decides whether K rises or falls with temperature, and give an industrial example such as ammonia synthesis.

bank.q: Using the Jacobian method and a Maxwell relation, derive an expression for the Joule–Thomson coefficient in terms of P–V–T data and Cp, and judge why hydrogen must be pre-cooled before throttling in a liquefaction plant.
outline: Write μ = (∂T/∂P)_H = −(∂H/∂P)_T / Cp.
Expand (∂H/∂P)_T = V − T(∂V/∂T)_P using the chain rule for Jacobians.
Obtain μ = [T(∂V/∂T)_P − V]/Cp.
For an ideal gas μ = 0; for a real gas its sign depends on whether the fluid is above or below its inversion temperature.
Hydrogen has an inversion temperature below room temperature, so throttling warms it unless it is cooled first; connect this to the Linde liquefaction cycle.

glossary.def: A property independent of the size of the system, such as temperature, pressure or molar volume.
A property that scales with the amount of material, such as total volume, internal energy or entropy.
A property whose change depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken.
A differential expression whose integral between two states is path independent.
The partial molar Gibbs free energy, equal to (∂G/∂n_i) at constant T, P and other mole numbers.
An effective pressure that replaces the true pressure in the ideal-gas chemical-potential formula, so that real-fluid behaviour is retained.
The ratio φ = f/P, tending to 1 as pressure tends to zero.
Z = PV/(RT); equal to 1 for an ideal gas and different from 1 for a real gas.
A relation among P, V and T for a fluid, such as the ideal-gas, van der Waals or Peng–Robinson equation.
Liquid at its boiling point for the given pressure, with quality zero.
Vapour at its condensation point for the given pressure, with quality one.
Vapour at a temperature above its saturation temperature for the given pressure.
Liquid at a temperature below its saturation temperature for the given pressure.
Enthalpy change when unit mass changes from saturated liquid to saturated vapour at constant temperature and pressure.
The single temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium.
The highest temperature and pressure at which liquid and vapour can be distinguished; above it there is one fluid phase.
A plot such as a T–s, P–h or Mollier diagram from which properties can be read graphically.
The temperature below which a gas cools on isenthalpic throttling and above which it warms.
The identity (∂x/∂y)_z (∂y/∂z)_x (∂z/∂x)_y = −1 for three variables linked by a state relation.
κ = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)_T, a positive quantity measuring volume change under pressure at fixed temperature.
α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)_P, the fractional volume change per kelvin at constant pressure.
A property divided by its critical value, such as T_r = T/T_c, used in generalized correlations.
The principle that fluids at the same reduced temperature and reduced pressure have similar properties.
